title: Project Kinetica — From Impact Iteration to Final Technical Art Breakdown
summary: A brief retrospective on separating collision controls, refining material response, and presenting the frozen study through the Showcase and Breakdown.

body.heading: Separate the controls
paragraphs: Project Kinetica connects weapon motion, impact evaluation, localized vertex deformation and material-specific particles. One recorded iteration separated contact area from collision radius: broad weapons could otherwise register contact too early. Keeping those controls separate allowed collision thickness to change without changing the pressure model.

body.heading: Refine the visible response
paragraphs: Slime’s topology and normals were revised to address faceting and uneven highlights. Carapace became Metal so the target and its spark effect expressed the same material idea. These iterations made geometry, naming and visible feedback part of the same authored response.

body.heading: Present the study with its limits
paragraphs: The final presentation brings together a Showcase, Technical Breakdown and public selected source tied to the frozen implementation. The comparison frames show authored responses rather than controlled physical measurements. Vertex displacement does not change topology or collision geometry, and no performance benchmark is claimed.

The retrospective ends at that frozen study. Its useful lesson is to explain both the visible result and the controls behind it; implementation detail and supporting evidence remain in the case study and Breakdown.

title: Project Confluence — From Technical Experiments to District Blockout
summary: The first development phase of Project Confluence connects climate-adaptive urban design with practical UE5 experiments in parameter-driven construction, environmental materials, rendering, and district blockout.

hero.alt: Early Unreal Engine 5 coastal district graybox with terraced terrain, white building masses and a provisional local rail corridor beside the ocean.
hero.caption: Project Confluence · Early coastal district blockout in Unreal Engine 5.

body.heading: Establish an environment direction
paragraphs: Project Confluence is an ongoing Environment Technical Art study exploring climate-adaptive high-density urbanism. It imagines a future city that continuously adapts its inherited infrastructure, combining mountainous island settlements, dense mixed-use development, ecological infrastructure, and rail-based public transportation. Local trams follow the islands' urban corridors, while cross-sea railways form a separate regional network.

The current production focus is a single representative coastal district. The aim is to establish a coherent relationship between steep terrain, everyday urban life, public transportation, and the ocean. An early District Master Plan explores how the station, neighborhood streets, residential areas, public spaces, and vertical circulation might connect across three terrain levels. These arrangements remain planning proposals to be validated in Unreal Engine.

body.heading: Explore parameter-driven construction
paragraphs: Early Blueprint workflow experiments were developed in a separate UE5 sandbox before formal environment production began. One procedural Actor uses exposed module count, mesh, and spacing parameters to construct repeated Static Mesh Components in the editor. Its Construction Script regenerates the arrangement when those parameters change, allowing the layout to be adjusted without manually replacing each component.

The comparison shows how a small set of parameters can produce different arrangements from the same construction logic. This establishes an initial parameter-driven workflow; procedural city generation has not yet been implemented.

images.alt: Focused Unreal Engine viewport showing five repeated mesh modules, with the original Spacing 150.0 and Module Count 5 parameters below.
Focused Unreal Engine viewport showing three repeated mesh modules, with the original Spacing 250.0 and Module Count 3 parameters below.

media.caption: Parameter-driven Blueprint construction · Five modules at spacing 150 compared with three modules at spacing 250.

media.alt: Blueprint graph looping from zero to module count minus one, adding Static Mesh Components, setting their mesh and placing them along Z using index multiplied by spacing.
media.caption: Construction Script logic · Module iteration, Static Mesh Component creation and relative positioning.

body.heading: Prototype environmental wetness
paragraphs: The next experiment focused on material behavior. An initial MF_WaterlineWetness prototype followed studies of Material Instances, Material Functions, UVs, and world-aligned mapping. The function calculates a height-based wetness mask using world-space position relative to an adjustable waterline, with noise controls introducing variation along the boundary and within the transition region.

The study compares the visible concrete material response with the underlying mask visualization to clarify how the wetness boundary behaves. It remains a material prototype; dynamic water simulation and a completed tidal system are outside its current scope.

images.alt: Close view of a concrete test surface showing the subtle height-based wetness response above and below its irregular transition.
Matching close view of the test surface with a diagnostic mask revealing the irregular waterline transition across both visible faces.

media.caption: Waterline wetness experiment · Concrete material response and diagnostic mask visualization.

body.heading: Investigate real-time rendering
paragraphs: Further experiments explored exposure, atmospheric fog, Lumen global illumination, reflections, and Nanite visualization. A simple red-surface lighting study was used to inspect how material color and indirect illumination influence surrounding surfaces. Together, these experiments provided an introduction to Unreal Engine's rendering workflow before beginning formal environment production.

media.alt: Red test column standing on a light floor in a simple Unreal Engine lighting study.
media.caption: Lumen lighting study · Red surface and surrounding floor used to inspect indirect illumination.

body.heading: Begin the coastal district blockout
paragraphs: Formal environment production began with the ProjectConfluence project and its first working level, L_District_Blockout_01, following the initial engine studies. The current Landscape covers approximately 252 × 504 meters, with three principal terrain elevations around 30m, 50m, and 70m. Initial graybox work establishes building masses, a local coastal tram corridor and station, bridge approaches, steep terrain, and distant-island context.

The blockout prioritizes terrain hierarchy, transit alignment, architectural massing, and the relationship between inhabited terraces and the ocean. Within that framework, the current planning iteration examines how the station area, middle neighborhood street, upper residential zone, and connecting pedestrian routes might form a coherent district. These circulation proposals remain under evaluation.

body.heading: Scope and next steps
paragraphs: Confluence remains in early development. The current district is a graybox environment, while the Blueprint, material, and rendering experiments were developed separately in the UE5 learning sandbox. Procedural city generation, dynamic water behavior, final environment assets, and the full transit system have not yet been implemented.

The next phase focuses on validating pedestrian circulation, architectural massing, terrain connections, and transit geometry before developing more advanced procedural environment tools. The objective is to resolve the district's fundamental spatial relationships and build a coherent, technically grounded environment before expanding the city.

title: Project Confluence — Spline-Based Procedural Infrastructure
summary: Exploring spline-driven infrastructure construction in Unreal Engine 5 through procedural mesh deformation, dynamic component generation, and fixed-interval instancing.

hero.alt: Unreal Engine 5 Blueprint viewport showing a curved spline infrastructure prototype with a continuous test mesh, repeated gray placeholder instances and a red direction arrow.
hero.caption: Spline-based infrastructure prototype · Continuous geometry and fixed-interval instances following an editable path.

body.heading: Establish a spline-based workflow
paragraphs: Following the initial district blockout, the next technical experiment explored how spline-driven construction could support infrastructure development in Project Confluence. The coastal district includes a local tram corridor whose alignment may need further adjustment as the surrounding environment develops.

The goal was to create a Blueprint prototype that could generate geometry along an editable spline and respond to path modifications directly in the Level Editor. Two complementary techniques were explored: Spline Mesh deformation for continuous infrastructure and Instanced Static Mesh placement for repeated elements.

body.heading: Read spatial data from a spline
paragraphs: The first experiment focused on spline control points, interpolation, and tangents. A Spline Component defines a continuous path but does not automatically deform attached geometry. An Arrow Component was used to visualize Location and Rotation sampled at a specified distance along the spline. These values were applied through the Construction Script, allowing the Arrow to follow the path's position and orientation.
This also introduced the importance of coordinate spaces. The Arrow experiment used world-space transforms, while the later mesh deformation workflow used local-space spline data.

body.heading: Generate continuous geometry
paragraphs: The next stage used Spline Mesh Components to deform geometry between adjacent spline points. Each segment receives start and end positions together with their corresponding tangents.

The initial test with Unreal Engine's default Cube produced substantial distortion around bends. Its limited subdivision density was insufficient to represent the curved deformation effectively. A replacement test mesh was created in Modeling Mode with additional longitudinal subdivisions. Its Forward Axis was then matched to the actual length direction of the asset, improving the deformation result.

After validating one segment, the Construction Script was extended with a For Loop. For an open spline containing N control points, the script generates N − 1 segments. Each iteration creates a new Spline Mesh Component and retrieves Location and Tangent from points i and i + 1. This allows the system to generate an entire continuous path without manually configuring individual segments. The resulting geometry was tested in the Level Editor and updated correctly when spline control points were modified.

media.alt: Blueprint loop creating Spline Mesh Components, assigning the test mesh and Y forward axis, and connecting local positions and tangents from consecutive spline points to Set Start and End.
media.caption: Procedural spline construction · Creating mesh components between consecutive spline points using their positions and tangents.

body.heading: Distribute fixed-size objects
paragraphs: Spline Mesh deformation works well for continuous surfaces, but embedded geometric details can stretch when segment lengths change. Repeated objects such as railway sleepers require a different approach. An Instanced Static Mesh Component was introduced to investigate fixed-interval placement.

The script derives the loop's final index by taking Floor of the spline length divided by an exposed Spacing parameter. Starting at index zero, each iteration samples Location and Rotation at a distance determined by the current index multiplied by Spacing. These values are combined into a Transform and passed to Add Instance. Previous instances are cleared before reconstruction to prevent duplication.

The Blueprint compiled successfully, and the resulting instances followed the test path. However, the placeholder geometry still showed orientation and presentation issues. This remains an instancing experiment rather than a finished railway asset.

media.alt: Blueprint clearing sleeper instances, deriving a loop bound from spline length divided by spacing, then adding world-space instances from sampled spline location and rotation with a fixed scale.
media.caption: Fixed-interval instancing · Sampling spline transforms and placing repeated instances through an exposed Spacing parameter.

body.heading: Geometry and coordinate considerations
paragraphs: Several implementation issues highlighted the importance of preparing geometry for procedural deformation. Insufficient mesh subdivision produced poor results around curved segments. Increasing longitudinal subdivision density improved the approximation of the spline. The mesh's Forward Axis also needed to match its actual length direction. The custom test mesh used Y as its deformation axis, while the instanced Cube followed its own local transform conventions.

Pivot placement and model orientation affected how geometry was positioned relative to the spline and how its dimensions appeared in the viewport. These observations reinforced the need for consistent asset conventions. Finally, the checker pattern on the deformed surface visibly stretched as spline segments changed length. This demonstrated why continuous geometry and repeated fixed-size components should not necessarily use the same generation method.

body.heading: Results and next steps
paragraphs: The experiment established a functional Blueprint prototype for editable spline-based geometry generation, combining continuous Spline Mesh segments with fixed-spacing Instanced Static Mesh placement. The continuous mesh workflow was validated through Level Editor modifications. The instancing workflow was implemented, but its visual presentation remains provisional.

The prototype is not a completed tram system. Production-ready track geometry, asset alignment, broader reuse testing, and integration into the coastal district remain future work. Vehicle movement, switches, and transport simulation were outside the scope of this experiment.

The primary outcome was a better understanding of spline data, procedural component creation, and instancing as practical tools for environment production. Future development will depend on Confluence's visual and production requirements rather than expanding the system unnecessarily.

title: Project Confluence — Developing the First Modular Facade Assets
summary: Developing the first facade modules in Blender, testing them in Unreal Engine 5, and using architectural context to guide a second set of window and full-height opening variations.

hero.alt: Unreal Engine 5 balcony facade with a framed window and full-height opening in adjacent wall units, showing the balcony floor, edge and surrounding blockout geometry.
hero.caption: Modular facade development in Unreal Engine 5 · Wall units and openings evaluated in their architectural context.

body.heading: Move from blockout to individual assets
paragraphs: After the spline infrastructure prototype, I shifted toward modular architecture. The aim was to begin producing architectural elements that could be evaluated in Confluence’s environment, bringing asset creation into the development process early. The first set consisted of a plain wall, a wall with a window opening, and a separate window frame. Working with a limited set kept the focus on modeling, UV preparation, and the transfer from Blender to Unreal before expanding the range of components.

body.heading: Establish the first Blender-to-Unreal pass
paragraphs: Preparing the initial assets involved working through wall openings, frame geometry, UVs, modifiers, and object origins. The first set was then exported from Blender and imported into Unreal Engine 5. In the initial engine test, the opening passed through the wall correctly, while the applied PBR material and texture scale appeared reasonable. This provided a working starting point for evaluating the assets inside the environment.
The important step was moving beyond an isolated model. Once the components were placed in an architectural arrangement, their proportions could be judged against the surrounding facade and balcony.

body.heading: Separate module size from opening size
paragraphs: The test supported keeping a 2-meter wall module as the base unit. A 4-meter balcony frontage could accommodate two units, providing space for a window and a full-height opening alongside each other. The initial 1.2 × 1.4-meter window appeared suitable for a side facade, but felt small on the balcony-facing elevation. This was less apparent at a medium viewing distance and more noticeable close up.

Rather than changing the entire wall module, I kept its width and developed alternative openings. The module establishes the assembly rhythm; the opening proportions respond to the particular facade condition.

images.alt: Front orthographic Unreal Engine view of the smaller framed window beside a full-height opening, with the wall seams and opening base providing a shared proportion reference.
Matching front orthographic view of the larger framed window beside the unchanged full-height opening, shown at the same scale as the smaller variation.

media.caption: Window proportion iteration · The smaller opening (left) and the larger variation (right), compared within the same balcony facade.

body.heading: Build the next opening variations
paragraphs: The next modeling pass added two opening sizes: 1.6 × 1.5 meters and 1.6 × 2.3 meters. Each variation included a matching wall, separate frame, and glass geometry, with UV preparation completed in Blender. The new frames also received a 45-degree angle-based smoothing treatment. This made shading preparation part of the asset workflow alongside geometry and UVs.

The larger window and full-height opening were then imported into Unreal and assembled into the balcony facade. Comparing the smaller and larger window in substantially the same view made the change in facade proportions easier to assess. They remain simple architectural components at this stage, without detailed opening mechanisms or hardware. To keep the growing set easy to navigate, I retained “Window” in the asset naming and used dimensions to distinguish the variations.

media.alt: Complete selected window-frame UV islands on the left and the complete orthographic frame mesh on the right, shown together in Blender.
media.caption: Window-frame UV preparation · The frame geometry and its UV layout inspected in Blender.

body.heading: What this stage establishes
paragraphs: This session produced an initial facade asset set, a first Blender-to-Unreal import test, and a second modeling and in-engine assembly pass informed by the proportions observed in the environment. It is still an early building kit. The work does not yet establish a complete residential building, a finished retrofit system, or a kit validated across the entire district. Glass geometry is part of the set, while its final in-engine appearance remains a separate material task.

The most useful lesson was to evaluate assets in context before expanding them. The first import made the components available in Unreal; the facade test gave the next modeling pass a concrete direction.

title: Project Confluence — Window Kit and Facade Assembly
summary: Developing a parameterized Blender tool for window-module preparation, checking the generated assets in Unreal Engine 5, and extending the workflow with adjustable Blueprint facade assembly.

hero.alt: Unreal Engine 5 perspective view of the existing balcony facade beside a repeated three-column, two-floor window assembly, with wall depth and provisional materials visible.
hero.caption: Facade assembly test in Unreal Engine 5 · Repeated window modules placed alongside the existing balcony facade.

body.heading: Identify the repeated preparation work
paragraphs: Following the first modular facade asset pass, the next step was to examine which parts of the workflow could be reused across opening variations. The wall, frame, and glass had related dimensions, while each variation also required UV preparation, consistent object origins, and export work. These repeated tasks provided a practical starting point for a small Blender tool, with the existing manually prepared assets serving as a reference for evaluating its output.

The aim was to make component preparation easier to adjust as the building developed. Opening proportions would still be judged in the environment, but producing another variation would no longer require working through every preparation step separately.

body.heading: Develop a parameterized Window Kit
paragraphs: With AI and Codex assistance, the repeated preparation workflow developed into Window Kit, a Blender add-on with a parameter panel and generation-and-export controls. I defined the module requirements, tested the panel, and used the generated results to check whether the tool preserved the intended asset conventions. The interface also brought the opening preset, module specifications, output mode, and run summary into one place, making the current configuration easier to review.

The tool connects geometry generation with asset preparation and export, while keeping the resulting assets available for inspection. This matters because a successful tool run is only one part of the workflow: the geometry, UVs, and placement conventions still need to behave as expected when the components are used in the environment.

media.alt: Blender view showing a complete wall, dark window frame and blue viewport glass beside the Window Kit parameter, Production export and run-summary interface.
media.caption: Window Kit in Blender · A wall, frame, and glass module shown alongside the tool’s parameter and export interface.

body.heading: Check the generated assets in Unreal
paragraphs: The October 31 inspection compared the generated components with the earlier manual workflow. For the checked 1.6 × 1.5-meter window variation, the generated wall had the expected pivot placement, the UVs reviewed in Blender appeared consistent with the manual baseline, and the glass geometry had also been unwrapped. The generated assets were then tested in Unreal Engine 5, with no obvious issues found in the inspected use.

This established a working path from the Blender tool to an in-engine module that could be used for further assembly. The facade remained in a structural testing stage, with provisional material appearances; the check concerned the generated components and their use in the scene rather than a finished surface treatment or validation of every possible tool configuration.

body.heading: Extend the workflow with facade assembly
paragraphs: Once the generated components were available in Unreal, the next task was to repeat them without positioning every wall, frame, and glass element individually. BP_ModularFacade was developed as a two-dimensional assembly prototype, using separate Instanced Static Mesh components for the three mesh groups. Corresponding instances share the same grid positions, allowing the components to form repeated window modules across columns and floors.

All three component groups were tested successfully, and changes to the Columns and Floors parameters updated the arrangement as expected. The recorded configurations include five columns across two floors and eight columns across three floors, demonstrating how the current module can form different facade extents through the same assembly logic. At this stage, the Blueprint repeats one complete window-module set; selecting and combining different module types remains the next development step.

images.alt: Complete five-column, two-floor facade array with the original Columns 5 and Floors 2 settings below, alongside module width 200.0 and height 320.0.
Complete eight-column, three-floor facade array at a different viewport scale, with Columns 8, Floors 3, module width 200.0 and height 320.0 settings below.

media.caption: Facade array configurations · Five columns across two floors, compared with eight columns across three floors.

body.heading: Results and next steps
paragraphs: This stage connects component preparation in Blender with repeated assembly in Unreal. Window Kit provides an adjustable way to generate the assets, while BP_ModularFacade controls their distribution across a facade. AI and Codex assisted with tool implementation; my work focused on defining the requirements, testing the output, working through the Blueprint assembly logic, and evaluating the results against Confluence’s architectural needs.

The current result is a tested generation-and-assembly workflow for the inspected window module, with working column and floor controls. Time savings and rendering performance have not been measured. The next step is to introduce module-type selection and evaluate the assembly within a more representative building arrangement, with material refinement following the structural work.
